title: The blind parents' curse
word: Dasharatha's death and the curse that
hookLine: a prince carries a water pot to a hut where two blind parents are waiting for their son
carry: amends begin with telling the truth
tomorrow: who was the boy at the river?

lines: MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.
cards: The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents.
They're old, and both blind, sitting in a hut nearby, thirsty, waiting for me to bring water. Go to them. Tell them.
Then he asks one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die.
He does it anyway, because he was asked.

teach.h: WHY ARE YOU SO LATE, SON?
teach.b: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son?
Your mother was worried. Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, mistaken for the son he has just killed.

teach.h: HE COULD SLIP AWAY. HE TELLS THEM.
teach.b: He could set the pot down and slip away. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the father answers with something striking.
Because you told us yourself, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, far worse would have followed. The parents ask to be taken to their son.
They sit with his body by the river, touching his face, grieving aloud.

teach.h: YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.
teach.b: Then the father speaks the words that will shape Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, you too will one day die grieving for a son.
And the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold both halves, because Hinduism does.

teach.h: PRAYASHCHITTA: AMENDS BEGIN WITH THE TRUTH.
teach.b: Making amends for a wrong is called prayashchitta, and it starts with owning the wrong out loud. The Manusmriti, one of the old law books, lists confession among its first steps, beside repentance.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SPARED HIM. THE CURSE CAME.
teach.b: Telling the truth spared the young prince that night. It didn't cancel the karma. And tonight, with Rama gone and his own life fading, the old king tells Kausalya the curse is coming true.

how: This episode is often told on its own as a story about duty to parents, and about a prince who told a blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

games.q: what does “dasharatha's death and the curse that” mean?
o: a goddess's curse that Ayodhya will fall to its enemies
a sage's curse that the king will never have any sons
a blind father's curse: you too will die grieving for a son

games.q: at the hut — tap the pairs.
p: asks the prince to take water to his parents
why are you so late, son?
you too will die grieving for a son

s: he asks him to take water to his blind parents and pull out the arrow.
the father says the confession spared the prince something worse
because he told them himself, the father says, he is still alive.
the old parents are both blind
they wait in a hut for their son to bring water.

games.q: you're the prince, at the hut with the water pot. the old father thinks you're his son. nobody saw what happened. what do you do?
o: set the pot down and leave quietly.
pretend to be the son for the night.
games.why: he tells them everything. the father says that's why he still lives. then comes the curse.

practice: Think of something small you once got wrong and never quite said out loud, something you can hold gently. Picture telling it plainly to the person it touched, nothing added, nothing hidden. That's where prayashchitta begins.
Notice how it feels just to imagine saying it straight.

wordCard.voice: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it. The blind father's words: as I die grieving for my son, you too will die grieving for a son.

orig.note: Sanskrit śāpa: a curse. the king tells this one as a curse he knows is coming true.

carryVoice: Your line: amends begin with telling the truth. The truth spared him once, but the curse still came. That's day five hundred forty-three.
